propositions.text: The Appellant is a Mexican citizen fearing harm from organized crime who killed his half-sister and threats from a former supervisor in Canada.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a Mexican citizen who alleges that he fears being harmed in Mexico by members of an organized crime group who killed his half-sister. He further alleges that he fears he would be harmed because of threats made by a former work supervisor in Canada after the Appellant reported this man's unlawful activities.

propositions.text: The Appellant came to Canada in 2019 and claimed refugee protection in October 2019.
propositions.quote: The Appellant came to Canada in XXXX 2019 and made a claim for refugee protection in October 2019.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges fear of harm from organized crime in Mexico and threats in Canada, and claimed refugee protection in 2019.

propositions.text: The RPD heard and rejected the Appellant's claim in 2020, focusing on credibility, delay, and internal flight alternative (IFA).
propositions.quote: The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) heard the Appellant's claim on September 23, 2020 and rejected it on October 28, 2020. The determinative issues were credibility, delay in making a claim, and internal flight alternative (IFA).

paragraphs.summary: The RPD rejected the Appellant's claim in 2020 based on credibility, delay, and IFA issues.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD made unreasonable findings and failed to properly consider evidence on IFA.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that the RPD made unreasonable and incorrect findings and failed to properly consider the evidence when applying the IFA test.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD erred in findings and evidence consideration on IFA.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed; the RPD was correct that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal. The determinative issue is IFA. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The appeal is dismissed; the RPD's decision on IFA and protection status is upheld by the court.

propositions.text: The Appellant seeks to rely on new evidence in this appeal, submitting an Affidavit sworn December 23, 2020.
propositions.quote: The Appellant seeks to rely on new evidence in this appeal.2 He has submitted an Affidavit, sworn by the Appellant on December 23, 2020.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant seeks to introduce new evidence via a December 2020 Affidavit.

propositions.text: New evidence is admissible if it arose after the RPD decision, was not reasonably available then, or could not reasonably have been provided before.
propositions.quote: According to the law,4 I can accept the evidence only if: i. it arose after the RPD decision; or ii. it was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or iii. the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected to provide it before the decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the legal criteria for admitting new evidence on appeal.

propositions.text: If new evidence meets one requirement, the court must decide it is new, credible, and relevant before acceptance.
propositions.quote: If the evidence meets at least one of these requirements, I must decide that the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.

paragraphs.summary: The court must find new evidence new, credible, and relevant before accepting it.

propositions.text: The Affidavit is admitted as new evidence because it arose after the RPD decision and is credible and relevant.
propositions.quote: I admit the Affidavit as new evidence. In his Affidavit, the Appellant states that on December 10, 2020 he was informed that his former work supervisor, XXXX, was asking for his contact information and is upset about business losses for which he blames the Appellant. The evidence in the Affidavit arose after the date of the RPD's decision so it is admissible under subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).6 It is new and I find that it passes the threshold for credibility and is relevant to the Appellant's claim because he alleges that XXXX is an agent of harm.

paragraphs.summary: The court admits the Affidavit as new, credible, and relevant evidence arising after the RPD decision.

propositions.text: The Appellant requests an oral hearing to test hearsay evidence in the Affidavit and argues it raises a serious credibility issue central to the claim.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has requested an oral hearing.7 He argues that the hearsay evidence in his Affidavit is based on his information and belief and should be admitted and tested for credibility at an oral hearing. The Appellant argues that the evidence raises a serious issue as to his credibility and that it is central to the decision on his claim because it demonstrates a continued interest in the Appellant by an alleged agent of persecution and would potentially justify accepting the claim.

propositions.text: The court is not persuaded by the Appellant's argument for an oral hearing.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded by the Appellant's argument.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant requests an oral hearing to test new evidence; the court rejects this request.

propositions.text: The new evidence shows the supervisor's interest but does not justify allowing or rejecting the claim without more evidence of harm in Mexico.
propositions.quote: Although the new evidence has the potential to support the Appellant's allegation that he fears XXXX and that XXXX is interested in him, acceptance of this evidence would not justify allowing or rejecting the claim.

propositions.text: The court finds no discrepancies requiring an oral hearing and can weigh the evidence without one.
propositions.quote: I find no discrepancies in the evidence that I would need to ask the Appellant about, as a matter of procedural fairness. I am able to consider and weigh the new evidence without an oral hearing.

propositions.text: Evidence of XXXX's interest is not determinative as no evidence links XXXX to harm in Mexico; no other evidence was submitted.
propositions.quote: Evidence of XXXX interest in contacting the Appellant could not be determinative of the claim, given that the Appellant has presented no evidence that XXXX has connections to anyone in Mexico who could harm the Appellant.9 If the Appellant has other evidence that supports his allegation that XXXX would harm him in Mexico, he could have applied to present it as new evidence. He has not done so.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the new evidence insufficient to affect the claim and denies the need for an oral hearing.

propositions.text: The Affidavit does not raise a serious credibility issue to justify allowing or rejecting the claim.
propositions.quote: I do not find that the Appellant's Affidavit raises a serious issue with respect to the Appellant's credibility that would justify allowing or rejecting his claim.

propositions.text: The request for an oral hearing is denied.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the request for an oral hearing is denied.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no serious credibility issue and denies the oral hearing request.

propositions.text: The RAD's role is to review all evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.
propositions.quote: The role of the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is to look at all the evidence and decide whether the RPD made the correct decision.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD reviews all evidence to determine if the RPD decision was correct.

propositions.text: The RPD correctly found a viable IFA in Merida or Campeche; the court will address Appellant's arguments on IFA and credibility concerns.
propositions.quote: The RPD correctly found that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Merida or Campeche. As IFA is the determinative issue, I will address those of the Appellant's arguments that pertain to the viability of the IFA. This includes the arguments aimed at four credibility concerns expressed by the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD correctly found a viable IFA and will address related arguments.

propositions.text: The IFA test has two prongs: no serious possibility of persecution or risk under section 97 IRPA; and conditions must not be unreasonable for claimant to live there.
propositions.quote: There are two prongs to the legal test for a viable IFA.12 The first prong requires that there be no serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, no risk under section 97 of the IRPA, meaning no danger of torture, risk to life, or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

propositions.text: The second prong requires that living conditions in the IFA not be unreasonably adverse, requiring proof of jeopardy to life or safety.
propositions.quote: The second prong requires that conditions in the IFA be such that it would not be unreasonable in all the circumstances, including personal circumstances, for the claimant to go and live there. The standard is high and requires proof of adverse conditions that would jeopardize the life and safety of the claimant in travelling to and living in the IFA location.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the two-prong legal test for a viable IFA under IRPA.

propositions.text: The RPD correctly found no serious possibility of persecution or section 97 risk in Merida or Campeche.
propositions.quote: The RPD correctly found that the Appellant would not face a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, a section 97 risk in Merida or Campeche

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found no serious persecution or risk in Merida or Campeche, which the court accepts.

propositions.text: The RPD concluded no serious possibility of persecution or section 97 risk if Appellant relocated to Merida or Campeche.
propositions.quote: The RPD concluded that the Appellant did not establish that he would face a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture, if he relocated to Merida or Campeche.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD's conclusion is incorrect.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that this is incorrect.

propositions.text: The court finds no error in the RPD's conclusion and independently finds the IFA viable under the first prong.
propositions.quote: I find no error in the RPD's conclusion. On an independent assessment, I find that the Appellant has not established that an IFA is not viable on the basis of the first prong of the test. My reasons follow.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found no serious risk in IFA; the Appellant disagrees; the court finds no error and agrees IFA is viable.

propositions.text: The RPD found insufficient credible evidence that cartel members pursue the Appellant.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that there was insufficient credible evidence to support a finding that the Appellant is being pursued by cartel members.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD ignored evidence of targeting by criminal group members.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that the RPD ignored evidence that he has been targeted by people connected to a criminal group.

propositions.text: The court independently finds the Appellant has not established on balance of probabilities that cartel members pursue him.
propositions.quote: On an independent assessment, I find that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that people connected to a cartel or organized crime group are motivated to pursue him.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found no credible evidence of cartel pursuit; the Appellant disagrees; the court agrees with the RPD.

propositions.text: The Appellant's sister was violently killed in 2017 in Chiapas.
propositions.quote: I accept, for purposes of the analysis, that the Appellant's sister was violently attacked and killed in XXXX 2017 in Chiapas.

propositions.text: The RPD's finding of no pursuit was based on credibility concerns with the Appellant's evidence.
propositions.quote: The RPD's finding that the Appellant failed to establish that he was being pursued by cartel members flowed from a series of credibility concerns with the Appellant's evidence.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD's credibility concerns lack merit.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that these credibility concerns lack merit.

propositions.text: The court is not persuaded by the Appellant's arguments against the credibility concerns.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded by his arguments.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant's sister was killed; the RPD found credibility issues; the Appellant disputes; the court is not persuaded.

propositions.text: The RPD drew a negative inference from the Appellant's inconsistent and speculative evidence about who killed his sister.
propositions.quote: The RPD drew a negative inference from the Appellant's inconsistent and speculative evidence about who is responsible for killing his sister.

propositions.text: The Appellant acknowledges speculation about naming two cartels but argues evidence shows threats from criminal organization members.
propositions.quote: The Appellant acknowledges that his testimony naming two cartels was speculative. He argues that this should not undermine the fact that there is evidence indicating that individuals who threatened him were part of a criminal organization in Mexico.

propositions.text: The court finds the Appellant's argument assumes the threat is established, which is unfounded; the onus is on the Appellant to prove credible threat evidence.
propositions.quote: This argument rests on assuming that it has been established as a fact that the Appellant has been threatened and that the only issue is the identity of those who threatened him. The assumption is unfounded. The onus is on the Appellant to establish that he faces a threat by presenting credible evidence.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues it may be impossible to know which group targets him.
propositions.quote: The Appellant further argues that it may be impossible to know which group is targeting him.

propositions.text: The court finds the RPD's credibility concern about speculation on the agent of persecution is not erroneous.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellant failed to establish that he was targeted. This finding was based, in part, on a credibility concern arising out of his speculation as to the identity of the alleged agent of persecution. I find no error in the RPD's assessment of this evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD negatively inferred from speculative evidence; the Appellant argues threats exist but court finds no error in RPD's credibility concerns.

propositions.text: The panel instructed the Appellant to say if he did not know an answer rather than guess.
propositions.quote: Before beginning to question the Appellant about his claim, the panel member told the Appellant to say if he did not know the answer to a question, rather than trying to guess.

propositions.text: The Appellant testified his life is in danger from two cartels but admitted speculation and uncertainty about their involvement.
propositions.quote: The Appellant then testified that his life is in danger in Mexico. Asked from whom, he said there were two cartels, namely, the Gulf Cartel and the Beltran Leyva Organization. When the panel asked the Appellant why he did not mention these groups in his Basis of Claim Form narrative, he said it was because he was not sure. The Appellant then acknowledged that he did not know if those cartels were involved and he was speculating.

propositions.text: The Appellant's immediate naming of two cartels after being told not to guess undermines his credibility about being targeted by criminal organizations.
propositions.quote: I find the Appellant's reference to two specific cartels immediately after being instructed not to guess at his answers undermines the credibility of his allegation that he has been targeted by members of a criminal organization.

paragraphs.summary: The panel instructed the Appellant not to guess; he named two cartels but admitted speculation; the court finds this undermines credibility.

propositions.text: RPD erred in finding Appellant's evidence about threatening note on sister's body not plausible
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in finding the Appellant's evidence that the alleged agents of persecution left a threatening note on his sister's body was not plausible.

propositions.text: RPD incorrectly relied on implausibility regarding threatening note evidence
propositions.quote: I accept the Appellant's argument that the RPD incorrectly relied on implausibility.

propositions.text: Organized crime groups in Mexico leave messages on women's bodies
propositions.quote: There is evidence that organized crime groups in Mexico engage in the practice of leaving messages on women's bodies.

propositions.text: Error is non-determinative; Appellant has not established on balance of probabilities that threatening note was left on sister's body
propositions.quote: I find the error non-determinative. On an independent assessment, I find that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that a note threatening her family was left on his sister's body.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RPD erred on threatening note plausibility; court accepts error but finds Appellant did not prove note was left on sister's body.

propositions.text: Appellant's father identified sister's body and saw the note
propositions.quote: The Appellant's Memorandum states that the Appellant's father identified the body of the Appellant's sister and saw the note

propositions.text: No evidence that Appellant's father saw the note
propositions.quote: I do not find that there is evidence indicating that the Appellant's father saw the note.

propositions.text: Father identified body; officer explained condition including message on chest
propositions.quote: The Appellant's evidence in his narrative is that his father identified the body and the officer in charge explained the condition in which the body was found, including the message left on her chest

propositions.text: Family did not report incident to police; told when, how, where sister died
propositions.quote: In his testimony, the Appellant explained that his family did not report the incident to the police; rather, when his sister's body was returned to the family, they were told when, how, and where she died.

propositions.text: Letter from father and sister's mother does not mention note or threats
propositions.quote: The letter from the Appellant's father and the mother of the Appellant's sister in support of the Appellant's claim does not refer to a note nor does it refer to threats against family members.

propositions.text: Letter states authorities received threats from organized crime and no follow up
propositions.quote: The letter states that there was no follow up by the authorities as the authorities received threats from organized crime.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant says father saw note; court finds no evidence father saw note; family told by officer about message; letter does not mention note or threats but says authorities received threats.

propositions.text: Evidence does not establish on balance of probabilities that threatening note was left on sister's body
propositions.quote: I find that the evidence does not, on a balance of probabilities, establish that a note threatening the Appellant's sister's family was left on her body.

propositions.text: No evidence any family member harmed or threatened since sister's death except Appellant
propositions.quote: The Appellant has also presented no evidence that any member of the Appellant's family or his brother-in-law's family has been harmed since his sister was killed nor has he presented evidence that any family member other than himself has been threatened.

propositions.text: RPD correctly found Appellant failed to establish multiple threatening phone calls
propositions.quote: The RPD correctly found that the Appellant failed to establish that he received multiple threatening telephone calls, as alleged

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no evidence note was left or family harmed/threatened; RPD correctly found no proof of multiple threatening calls.

propositions.text: RPD found Appellant embellished evidence about receiving threats
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellant embellished his evidence about receiving threats.

propositions.text: Appellant argues he was confused and reasonably explained inconsistencies
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that he was confused at the hearing and that he reasonably explained the inconsistencies in his evidence.

propositions.text: On independent assessment, RPD was correct that Appellant did not establish threatening calls two or three times a week
propositions.quote: On an independent assessment, I find that the RPD was correct to conclude that the Appellant has not, on a balance of probabilities, established his allegation that he received threatening phone calls two or three times a week before he left Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found Appellant embellished threats; Appellant claims confusion; court agrees RPD was correct on threatening calls evidence.

propositions.text: Appellant received threatening call same day he visited authorities in Chiapas
propositions.quote: The Appellant's evidence, in his Basis of Claim Form narrative dated October 6, 2019, refers to him receiving a threatening telephone call on the same day that he went to investigating authorities in Chiapas

propositions.text: Caller knew file, told him to drop investigation, asked about brother-in-law, threatened family
propositions.quote: His evidence is that the call came from someone who: was familiar with the file, told him to drop the investigation, asked about his brother-in-law's whereabouts, and said that, if they continued with the case, another family member would be killed.

propositions.text: Appellant hung up; phone kept ringing but he did not answer
propositions.quote: The Appellant states that he hung up and that the phone kept ringing but he did not want to answer.

propositions.text: In March 2020 amendments, Appellant states he received threatening calls two or three times a week before leaving Mexico
propositions.quote: In amendments to his narrative, dated March 9, 2020, the Appellant states that before he left for Canada he was receiving threatening phone calls approximately twice or three times a week.

propositions.text: Callers said they knew where he and family lived and threatened him
propositions.quote: He states that the callers would say they knew where he and his family lived and, if his family died, it would be the Appellant's fault.

propositions.text: Callers told him to stop investigation or he would be next
propositions.quote: The Appellant states that they told him to stop the investigation and if he did not he would be next because they knew where he was.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant's narrative says he got threatening call day he visited authorities; later amended to say calls were frequent before leaving Mexico.

propositions.text: At hearing, Appellant said calls began when he hired lawyer
propositions.quote: At the hearing, the Appellant was asked to explain the difference between his evidence in the initial narrative and in his amended narrative. He testified that the calls began when he hired the lawyer.

propositions.text: Appellant testified calls started when he started the procedure
propositions.quote: The panel repeated the question and the Appellant testified that the calls started when he started the procedure.

propositions.text: Appellant said one call in initial narrative was interpreter confusion; calls he refers to started when he hired lawyer
propositions.quote: In later questioning by counsel about why he mentioned only one call in his initial narrative, the Appellant testified that he thought "they got confused when the[y] did the interpretation" and the one call was a reference to the call made by the Appellant's neighbour to tell him that people were walking around his parcel of land and the calls that the Appellant is talking about are the ones he received when he hired the lawyer.

paragraphs.summary: At hearing, Appellant said calls began when he hired lawyer; said initial narrative's one call was interpreter confusion.

propositions.text: No indication Appellant was confused at hearing; he understood questions
propositions.quote: I have listened to the audio recording of the hearing and I find no indication that the Appellant was confused.

propositions.text: Appellant suggested interpreter error but no evidence supports this
propositions.quote: No evidence has been presented to support the Appellant's suggestion that the interpreter erred.

propositions.text: Interpreter declared full interpretation; Appellant assured understanding
propositions.quote: The initial narrative is accompanied by an interpreter's declaration indicating that the content was fully interpreted to the Appellant who assured the interpreter that he understood it.

propositions.text: Interpreter error cannot explain confusion or omission in narratives
propositions.quote: I do not see how an error by the interpreter could explain confusion between these events nor how it could explain the omission of the information that the Appellant added in his amended narrative.

propositions.text: Agree with RPD that Appellant failed to reasonably explain differences and embellished evidence
propositions.quote: I agree with the RPD that the Appellant failed to reasonably explain the difference between his initial narrative and his amendments to the narrative and that he embellished his evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no confusion or interpreter error; agrees with RPD that Appellant embellished evidence and failed to explain differences.

propositions.text: Appellant argues evidence consistently shows calls began when he hired lawyer
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that his evidence is consistent that the threatening phone calls began when he hired the lawyer to investigate his sister's case.

propositions.text: Evidence does not reflect calls began when lawyer hired; that is hearing testimony
propositions.quote: I do not find that this correctly reflects his evidence. It reflects his testimony at the hearing.

propositions.text: Narrative states first call was in Chiapas when authorities lost sister's file; later he hired lawyer in Tabasco
propositions.quote: However, in his narrative, he states that he received the first call in Chiapas on the day he was told by the authorities that they had lost his sister's file. His evidence in the narrative is that later when he returned to Tabasco, he hired a lawyer.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues calls began when lawyer hired; court finds narrative shows first call earlier in Chiapas, lawyer hired later in Tabasco.

propositions.text: Claimant can amend Basis of Claim Form without adverse credibility inference
propositions.quote: I recognize that a claimant has the right to make amendments to their Basis of Claim Form and that this will not necessarily lead to an adverse credibility inference.

propositions.text: Significant difference between single call on day of visit and multiple calls weeks before departure
propositions.quote: However, I find there is a significant difference between the evidence of a single threatening phone call on the day the Appellant visited the investigating authorities in Chiapas, and the evidence of two or three threatening phone calls a week between December 2018 and March 2019, when the Appellant left his home in Tabasco to come to Canada.

propositions.text: Difference is material to motivation of agent of persecution
propositions.quote: The difference is material to the issue of the motivation of the agent of persecution to pursue the Appellant.

propositions.text: On independent assessment, Appellant has not established on balance of probabilities that he received frequent threatening calls before departure
propositions.quote: On an independent assessment, I find that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that he received the threatening phone calls he alleges that he was receiving in the months before his departure from Mexico.

propositions.text: Supporting evidence does not establish continuing threat from sister's killers
propositions.quote: The Appellant's supporting evidence does not establish a continuing threat from his sister's killers.

paragraphs.summary: Court recognizes right to amend claim but finds material difference between single and frequent calls; finds no proof of frequent calls or continuing threat.

propositions.text: Appellant argues RPD erred by not considering Mexican lawyer and neighbour evidence and contradicting it
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in failing to consider the evidence from the Mexican lawyer and the neighbour in Mexico and to make a finding contradicting this evidence.

propositions.text: RPD found insufficient credible evidence of jeopardy from sister's killers
propositions.quote: The RPD found that there was insufficient credible evidence that the Appellant would be in jeopardy at the hands of the alleged perpetrators of his sister's killing.

propositions.text: No requirement to refer to each piece of evidence or make specific findings on each
propositions.quote: There is no requirement to refer to each piece of evidence or to make specific findings about each piece of evidence tendered in support of a claim.

propositions.text: RPD's reasons reflect thorough engagement with evidence
propositions.quote: I find that the RPD's reasons reflect a thorough engagement with the evidence.

propositions.text: RAD's role is to conduct independent assessment, remedying any error
propositions.quote: In any event, it is the role of the RAD to conduct an independent assessment, which would remedy the error, had there been one.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RPD erred by ignoring lawyer and neighbour evidence; court finds RPD engaged evidence thoroughly and RAD will independently assess.

propositions.text: Lawyer withdrew from sister's case due to risk and advised Appellant it was wearisome and problematic
propositions.quote: The lawyer states that he withdrew from investigating the case of the Appellant's sister's death because he learned that the matter was risky and he advised the Appellant that the matter was wearisome and could cause them problems.

propositions.text: Appellant says lawyer withdrew in February 2019
propositions.quote: He does not state the date he withdrew from the matter but the Appellant's evidence is that it was in February 2019.

propositions.text: Neighbour states in June 2019 men in pickup and motorcycles asked about Appellant and family, offering money for info
propositions.quote: The Appellant's neighbour states that, in June 2019, three people in a pickup truck approached him one day, followed by two people on motorcycles days later, in each case asking where and when they could find the Appellant and his family, and in the latter case, offering $1,000 for the information.

propositions.text: Neighbour says one communicated by handheld radio
propositions.quote: The Appellant's neighbour states that one of them was communicating through a handheld radio.

propositions.text: Appellant says only government or cartels use handheld radios in Mexico
propositions.quote: The Appellant's evidence is that the only people who use handheld radios in Mexico are from the government or the cartels.

paragraphs.summary: Lawyer withdrew from case due to risk; neighbour reported men seeking Appellant in June 2019; handheld radios used by government or cartels.

propositions.text: Lawyer's letter does not corroborate continuing threat evidence
propositions.quote: I do not find that the lawyer's letter corroborates the Appellant's evidence of a continuing threat.

propositions.text: Investigation lost, family not pursuing, lawyer not investigating, Appellant dropped matter and would not pursue again
propositions.quote: The Appellant's evidence is that the investigating authorities have lost the file, his sister's parents are not pursuing the investigation, the lawyer is not investigating, and the Appellant dropped the matter and would not pursue it again if he were to return to Mexico.

propositions.text: Appellant and family took lawyer's advice
propositions.quote: The evidence is that the Appellant and his family have taken the lawyer's advice.

propositions.text: Lawyer's letter does not indicate threat continuation after investigation stopped
propositions.quote: The lawyer's letter does not indicate any continuation of a threat following the discontinuation of inquiries and investigation into the sister's death.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds lawyer's letter does not corroborate continuing threat; investigation stopped and Appellant dropped matter following lawyer's advice.

propositions.text: Neighbour's letter insufficient to support threat in IFA
propositions.quote: I find the neighbour's letter insufficient to support the existence of a threat to the Appellant in the IFA.

propositions.text: Appellant lived in Tacotalpa from 2001 to 2019
propositions.quote: The Appellant's address history indicates that he lived in XXXX XXXX XXXX Tacotalpa, Tabasco, from XXXX 2001 until his departure from Mexico in XXXX 2019.

propositions.text: Appellant says family relocated within Mexico
propositions.quote: The Appellant refers to the men searching for him after his family had been "relocated within Mexico".

propositions.text: Appellant's wife and children continued to live in Tacotalpa; he rented farm in Libertad
propositions.quote: The Appellant's evidence was that his wife and the children of their relationship continued to reside in Tacotalpa and that he rented a farm in Libertad, Tacotalpa.

propositions.text: Libertad is 20 km from Tacotalpa, population 1,042
propositions.quote: The evidence is that the village of Libertad is just over 20 kilometres away from the town of Tacotalpa and is in the municipality Tacotalpa, in the state of Tabasco. Information provided by the Appellant indicates that Libertad has a population of 1,042, an increase of 46 people from the year 2005.

propositions.text: No evidence men who inquired threatened family in Tabasco
propositions.quote: There is no evidence that the men who inquired after the Appellant approached or threatened his family in Tabasco.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds neighbour's letter insufficient to show threat; Appellant lived in Tacotalpa area; no evidence family threatened in Tabasco.

propositions.text: Appellant testified cartel did not act on threat because he moved
propositions.quote: He testified that the threat was more towards him. His testimony was that they did not carry out their threat because he moved.

propositions.text: Evidence does not indicate when Appellant and family moved
propositions.quote: The evidence does not indicate when the Appellant and his family moved.

propositions.text: Accept Appellant moved but not far; no allegation of hiding between sister's death and departure
propositions.quote: I accept the Appellant's evidence that he moved but the evidence is that he did not move far. The Appellant has not alleged that he lived in hiding between the date of his sister's death in April 2017 and his departure for Canada in XXXX 2019.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant testified cartel threat not acted on because he moved; court accepts move but not far and no hiding alleged.

propositions.text: Appellant has not established sister's killers motivated to locate him in Merida or Campeche
propositions.quote: I find that the Appellant has not established that whoever killed his sister is motivated to locate him in Merida or Campeche

propositions.text: No evidence killers located him before he left Mexico while living in small town for 18 years
propositions.quote: given that there is no evidence that they located him before he left Mexico while he continued to live in an area with a population of just over one thousand people where he had lived for almost 18 years.

propositions.text: Appellant's evidence does not establish killers motivated to pursue him despite no investigation
propositions.quote: The Appellant's evidence does not establish that his sister's killers are motivated to pursue him despite the absence of an investigation into her death.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Appellant has not established sister's killers motivated to find him; no evidence they located him before departure.

propositions.text: Investigation discontinued and not pursued by authorities or family
propositions.quote: The Appellant's evidence is that the investigation into his sister's death was discontinued and, according to the Appellant, is not being pursued by authorities or family members.

propositions.text: Appellant testified cartel pursues him because he can identify two men at sister's funeral and knows brother-in-law's whereabouts
propositions.quote: He testified that there are two reasons. One reason is because he can identify two men who attended his sister's funeral and he believes they are connected to his sister's killing. The other is that the cartels want to find his brother-in-law and they think the Appellant knows his brother-in-law's whereabouts.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant says investigation stopped; fears cartel pursues him because he can identify men and knows brother-in-law's whereabouts.

propositions.text: Appellant's evidence that cartel pursues him due to identification is speculative
propositions.quote: I find the Appellant's evidence that cartel members would pursue him because they fear he could identify people connected to his sister's death is speculative.

propositions.text: Appellant testified two men at funeral asked about brother-in-law and police presence
propositions.quote: He testified that two men who attended his sister's funeral told him they were friends of the family. He testified that they asked when the Appellant's brother-in-law would arrive and asked why there were police and journalists at the funeral.

propositions.text: Appellant recognized faces in police video and thinks they are assassins
propositions.quote: The Appellant's evidence is that he subsequently recognized their faces in a video shown to him by the police. He testified that he thinks they are the assassins.

propositions.text: Men were in truck outside sister's house morning of day she was killed
propositions.quote: His testimony was that they were in a truck that was outside his sister's house in the morning of the day that his sister was killed in the afternoon.

propositions.text: Appellant saw video 2-3 months after sister died; could not see faces exactly but knew it was them
propositions.quote: The Appellant testified that he saw the video two or three months after his sister died, he could not see their faces exactly, but he knew it was them because they were in the same truck.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Appellant's claim cartel pursues him due to identification is speculative; Appellant testified about men at funeral and video recognition.

propositions.text: Police no longer investigating sister's killing; dropped due to cartel influence
propositions.quote: The Appellant's evidence is that the police are no longer investigating the killing of the Appellant's sister. The Appellant alleges that the police have dropped the investigation because of the cartel's influence.

propositions.text: Speculative that ability to identify two men at funeral motivates cartel to look for Appellant in IFA
propositions.quote: Consequently, I find it speculative that his ability to identify two guests at the funeral as people who were in a truck outside his sister's home on the morning of the day she later died would motivate cartel members, who allegedly killed his sister, to look for the Appellant in the IFA.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant says police dropped investigation due to cartel; court finds speculative that identification motivates cartel to seek Appellant in IFA.

propositions.text: Appellant fears cartel wants to locate him because he knows brother-in-law's whereabouts
propositions.quote: The Appellant also testified that he fears the cartel wants to locate him because they think he knows the whereabouts of his brother-in-law.

propositions.text: Appellant testified life in danger because he told authorities brother-in-law would continue investigation
propositions.quote: He testified that if he had not told the authorities in December 2018 that his brother-in-law would continue to pursue the investigation, his life would not be in danger.

propositions.text: Court finds this speculative and inconsistent with argument that cartel can locate him anywhere in Mexico
propositions.quote: I find this speculative and inconsistent with the Appellant's argument that he cannot live safely in an IFA location because cartel members can locate him anywhere in Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant fears cartel wants him for brother-in-law info; court finds this speculative and inconsistent with claim cartel can find him anywhere.

propositions.text: Cartel members often can locate people when motivated
propositions.quote: I agree with the Appellant that there is evidence that, in many cases, cartel members are able to locate people when they are motivated to do so.

propositions.text: Appellant unsure of brother-in-law's real name due to multiple names and ties to cartel and gangs
propositions.quote: The Appellant's evidence is that he is not sure of his brother-in-law's real name as he used several names, because of his ties to the cartel and gangs in Mexico.

propositions.text: Appellant and family unaware of brother-in-law's human trafficking involvement until sister's death
propositions.quote: According to the Appellant, he and his family did not know about his brother-in-law's activities. His evidence is that they learned of his involvement in human trafficking only after the Appellant's sister was killed.

propositions.text: More likely cartel knows more about brother-in-law than Appellant and family
propositions.quote: The evidence is that it is more likely cartel members know more about the Appellant's brother-in-law than the Appellant does.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees cartel can locate people; Appellant unsure of brother-in-law's real name; family unaware of his trafficking; cartel likely knows more.

propositions.text: Cartel members think the Appellant knows his brother-in-law's whereabouts because he told authorities his brother-in-law would pursue the investigation.
propositions.quote: The only evidence the Appellant has provided in support of his allegation that cartel members think he knows his brother-in-law's whereabouts is that in December 2018 he told the investigating authorities that his brother-in-law would pursue the investigation.

propositions.text: This evidence does not establish on a balance of probabilities that cartel members believe the Appellant knows his brother-in-law's location.
propositions.quote: I find that this does not, on a balance of probabilities, establish that cartel members believe the Appellant knows where his brother-in-law is.

propositions.text: Accepting the Appellant's argument requires speculative assumptions about information flow and beliefs of cartel members.
propositions.quote: To reach that conclusion requires assuming that the authorities relayed that information to cartel members, that the cartel members believed that the Appellant was telling the truth about being in contact with his brother-in-law, and that the cartel members believed that the Appellant's brother-in-law had disclosed his location to the Appellant.

propositions.text: Findings must be based on evidence, not speculative assumptions.
propositions.quote: I am required to base my findings on the evidence and I find that the Appellant has not presented evidence to establish, on a balance of probabilities, the conclusions that I would need to reach to accept his argument.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges cartel members think he knows his brother-in-law's location, but the court finds this unproven and based on speculative assumptions.

propositions.text: Individuals found the Appellant's family in their safe location in Mexico.
propositions.quote: The Appellant also argues that individuals found the Appellant's family in the location where they had sought safety in Mexico.

propositions.text: The Appellant's family remained in the same small municipality where he lived for almost 18 years.
propositions.quote: his family remained in the same small municipality where the Appellant had been living for almost 18 years.

propositions.text: Cartel members could likely locate the Appellant in that municipality if motivated.
propositions.quote: I accept that the cartel members would likely be able to locate him in that municipality, if they were motivated to do so.

propositions.text: Absence of evidence that cartel located or approached the family indicates lack of interest in the Appellant and family.
propositions.quote: I find the absence of any evidence that they located him before he left Mexico or that they approached his family indicative of a lack of interest in the Appellant and his family.

propositions.text: Evidence does not establish that the sister's killers are motivated to locate the Appellant on a balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: The evidence does not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that his sister's killers are motivated to locate the Appellant

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues his family was found, but the court finds no evidence of cartel interest or motivation to locate him or his family.

propositions.text: Cartels in Mexico have many ways to locate people when motivated.
propositions.quote: I accept the evidence that cartels in Mexico have many ways to locate people, when they are motivated to do so.

propositions.text: The Appellant has not established that the killers are motivated to locate him in an IFA.
propositions.quote: I find that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that whoever killed his sister, allegedly members of a cartel or organized crime group, are motivated to locate him in an IFA.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant did not establish that XXXX has means and motivation to locate him in Mexico to harm him.
propositions.quote: The RPD correctly found that the Appellant did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that XXXX has the means and the motivation to locate the Appellant in Mexico in order to harm him

paragraphs.summary: The court accepts cartels can locate people but finds the Appellant did not prove killers are motivated to find him; the RPD's finding is correct.

propositions.text: The Appellant fears XXXX, a former Canadian workplace supervisor, who deceived him and threatened him after he reported XXXX to police.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleges that he fears XXXX, a former supervisor in a Canadian workplace. His evidence is that, after he arrived in Canada, XXXX got him a job with a XXXX XXXX and a place to live, although the Appellant did not have a work permit. The Appellant's evidence is that XXXX deceived him about Canadian immigration rules. The Appellant made a connection through his church with a refugee centre and a lawyer and encouraged other migrants not to give XXXX their money and not to follow his advice. As a result, XXXX threatened the Appellant and fired him from his job. The Appellant reported XXXX and his business to the police. In December 2020, the Appellant heard from former co-workers that XXXX was upset and asking around for the Appellant's contact information. The Appellant has been told that there are rumours circulating in the local Mexican community that the employer for whom the XXXX XXXX provided services was fined because of an investigation involving the Appellant and XXXX was upset that this would have an impact on his business.

propositions.text: For analysis, the court accepts these allegations as true.
propositions.quote: For the purposes of the analysis, I accept these allegations.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges fear of XXXX due to deception, threats, and police reports; the court accepts these allegations for analysis.

propositions.text: The Appellant fears harm from XXXX in Mexico and argues evidence of XXXX's continued interest justifies his claim.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleges that he will not be safe in Mexico because XXXX seeks to do him harm. The Appellant argues that the evidence of XXXX continued interest in him would potentially justify accepting his claim.

propositions.text: The RPD found insufficient credible evidence that XXXX has ability or interest to pursue the Appellant and family in Mexico.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that there was insufficient credible evidence to show that XXXX has the ability or the interest to pursue the Appellant and his family in Mexico.

propositions.text: The court finds no error in the RPD's conclusion and on independent assessment finds no evidence XXXX can locate or harm the Appellant in Mexico.
propositions.quote: I find no error in the RPD's conclusion. I have considered the new evidence submitted to the RAD, and on an independent assessment, I find that the Appellant has not established that XXXX has the ability to locate or harm the Appellant in an IFA location in Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant fears harm from XXXX in Mexico; the RPD found no credible evidence, and the court agrees on independent assessment.

propositions.text: Counsel acknowledged uncertainty whether XXXX poses risk in Mexico or has connections to harm the Appellant's family.
propositions.quote: Counsel's submissions to the RPD acknowledged that it was unclear whether the Appellant faces risk from XXXX in Mexico and that it was unknown whether XXXX actually has any connections to anyone in Mexico who could harm the Appellant's family.

propositions.text: Evidence of XXXX upset in Canada does not address gaps about his ability to harm the Appellant in Mexico.
propositions.quote: The evidence that XXXX has recently asked for the Appellant's contact information in Canada and is upset about possible business losses that he attributes to the Appellant does not address those gaps in the evidence.

propositions.text: The RPD correctly found the Appellant has not established it would be unreasonable to relocate to Merida or Campeche.
propositions.quote: The RPD correctly found that the Appellant has not established that, on a balance of probabilities, it would be unreasonable for him to relocate to Merida or Campeche

paragraphs.summary: Counsel acknowledged uncertainty about XXXX's risk in Mexico; the court finds evidence of XXXX upset in Canada insufficient and agrees relocation is reasonable.

propositions.text: The RPD found it would not be unreasonable for the Appellant to relocate to proposed IFA locations.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that it would not be unreasonable for the Appellant to relocate to one of the proposed IFA locations.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD erred in finding there is an IFA in Merida or Campeche.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that it was an error for the RPD to find that there is an IFA in Merida or Campeche.

propositions.text: On independent assessment, the court agrees with the RPD that it is not unreasonable to live in Merida or Campeche.
propositions.quote: On an independent assessment, for the reasons that follow, I agree with the RPD's conclusion that the evidence does not, on a balance of probabilities, establish that it would be unreasonable for the Appellant to go and live in Merida or Campeche.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found relocation reasonable; the Appellant argues error; the court independently agrees relocation to Merida or Campeche is reasonable.

propositions.text: The Appellant testified that the area around Campeche is very dangerous and far from where his sister died and he lived.
propositions.quote: The Appellant was asked if he could live safely in Merida or Campeche. He testified that where his sister died is seven hours from Campeche and where he lived is four hours from Campeche and the whole area is very dangerous.

propositions.text: The RPD noted crime increased in Merida and Campeche but country conditions show generally low crime there.
propositions.quote: The RPD considered the evidence that crime in Merida and Campeche had increased but noted that country conditions documentation indicates that it is generally low in the area.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues RAD jurisprudence shows Campeche and Merida are not free from violence and claimants targeted may be found there.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that the RAD's recent jurisprudence supports that Campeche and Merida are not free from violence but are places where claimants who have been targeted may be found.

propositions.text: An IFA need not be free of crime; that is not the test for reasonableness of relocation.
propositions.quote: As the RPD also noted, it is not necessary that an IFA be free of crime; that is not the test.

propositions.text: Each appeal is decided on its own facts; the cited decision concerns Jalisco Cartel's ability to locate a claimant they pursue.
propositions.quote: While administrative tribunals strive to promote consistency in decision-making, each appeal is decided on its own facts. Furthermore, the decision cited by the Appellant deals with the ability of the Jalisco Cartel New Generation to locate a claimant whom the cartel is motivated to pursue.

propositions.text: The Appellant has not established he would be pursued by cartel members.
propositions.quote: For the reasons I have already given, I find that the Appellant has not established that he would be pursued by cartel members.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant says Campeche and Merida are dangerous; the court notes crime is generally low and finds no evidence he would be pursued there.

propositions.text: The Appellant's submissions focus on safety of IFAs and made no other reasonableness submissions.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's submissions focus on the safety of the IFA locations. The Appellant made no other submissions at the RPD or the RAD about reasonableness of the IFAs.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant is a young man with work experience and relocation to IFAs is not objectively unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The RPD considered that the Appellant is a young man with work experience and concluded that it was not objectively unreasonable for him to move to one of the IFA locations, to be eventually joined by his wife and children.

propositions.text: On independent assessment, the court agrees relocation to Campeche or Merida is not objectively unreasonable.
propositions.quote: On an independent assessment, I come to the same conclusion as the RPD, namely that it is not objectively unreasonable for the Appellant to relocate to Campeche or Merida.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant focused on safety concerns; the RPD and court find relocation to Campeche or Merida not objectively unreasonable.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed and the RPD decision confirmed that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal and pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision denying refugee or protection status to the Appellant.
